implementation_notes: Modern C++ default: ip::tcp::acceptor is the acceptor, async_connect() the connector and io_context the dispatcher; the handler factory collapses into the accept/connect completion handler. The accept completion handler must schedule the next async_accept before returning, otherwise the server accepts only one connection. Keep the acceptor and session state alive until io_context finishes.
pitfalls: A single-threaded io_context must not run blocking work inside completion handlers.
Keep the socket and handler state alive across async_accept/async_connect; dangling completion state is a classic bug.

variants.name: Boost.Asio with C++20 stackless coroutines
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 stackless coroutines turn the callback chains into linear accept/connect loops; the roles stay the same but the completion-handler plumbing becomes ordinary control flow. Prefer where the toolchain is C++20 and the callback pyramid hurts readability.
pitfalls: Detached co_spawn erases ownership: the session coroutine must own its state; a coroutine referring to a dead connection object is the coroutine-era analogue of the dangling-completion bug.
Forget as_tuple() around async_accept and the error_code escapes as an exception instead.

variants.name: ACE Acceptor-Connector over the Reactor (classic)
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's classic home (POSA2, Schmidt et al.): ACE ships ACE_Acceptor / ACE_Connector handler skeletons that instantiate the full role structure (acceptor, connector, dispatcher, service handler) over its Reactor. Choose when ACE's service-configuration and policy layers are already in the stack.
pitfalls: ACE couples handlers to its Reactor/Service-Configurator machinery; prefer Asio unless ACE's policy layers are required.
